item.title: Local LLM VRAM Planning 2026: The KV Cache Math Behind the Context You Can Actually Serve
item.description: Does this model, quant and context fit your card? Compute weights plus KV from the model's own config at a pinned revision, with a per-model table, a hybrid-attention counterexample and a runnable planner.
item.content:encoded:
A model card says 40,960 tokens. The Q4_K_M file is 4.68 GiB. The card has 12 GB. You set -c 40960, and one of three things happens: the load fails, the runtime spills layers to CPU and tokens per second collapse, or the server starts and silently serves a shorter context than you asked for.

Which of the three you get depends on a number that appears in none of those three places — the key/value cache the runtime allocates at load time from the context you request. This page computes it for four specific models from their own config.json at a pinned revision, turns it into a “largest context that fits this card” table, and ships a planner you can run offline.

If you searched for benchmark charts, this page will disappoint you on purpose. There are no throughput measurements here: this environment has no GPU, and inventing a tokens-per-second table is worse than saying so. What is here is arithmetic you can check in a minute, plus the one failure mode that arithmetic gets wrong.

The budget is three terms

resident ≈ GGUF file size + KV cache at your context + runtime overhead

Only the first term is on the download page. The third term — compute buffers, CUDA context, the graph allocator — is machine- and backend-specific; the planner below takes it as a declared allowance and prints it separately, so you can see what you are assuming rather than have it hidden in a fudge factor.

The middle term is the one that changes with context:

bytes_per_token = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element

Two for key plus value. n_layers, n_key_value_heads and head_dim come from the model’s config.json — not from the parameter count, and not from the size of the file. Two 8B-class models can differ by 8× here depending on how many heads share keys and values.

Qwen3-8B, read from its config at revision b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218: 36 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, and max_position_embeddings 40,960. That is 2 × 36 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 147,456 bytes per token — 144 KiB — which is 0.56 GiB at 4,096 tokens and 5.62 GiB at the native 40,960.

Same model, same file, a cache five times larger than the weights at the context the card advertises. That is the whole trap in one number.

Four models, computed from their own configs

Every row below is computed at batch size 1 with an f16 cache, from the config fields saved at the revisions read on 2026-11-03, and the GGUF sizes are the published file sizes in the same repositories. None of it is a measured load.

Model Layers KV heads × head dim Native ctx f16 KV B/token KV at 8k KV at native Q4_K_M file
Qwen3-8B 36 8 × 128 40,960 147,456 1.12 GiB 5.62 GiB 4.68 GiB
Qwen3-14B 40 8 × 128 40,960 163,840 1.25 GiB 6.25 GiB 8.38 GiB
Devstral-Small-2507 40 8 × 128 131,072 163,840 1.25 GiB 20.0 GiB 13.35 GiB
Gemma 4 31B (hybrid) 60 16 × 256 262,144 see below 1.41 GiB 20.8 GiB 17.07 GiB

Config sources: Qwen3-14B, Devstral-Small-2507, Gemma 4 31B. The file-size column comes from one mirror per model, each an /api/models/<repo>/tree/main?blobs=true listing read on 2026-11-03: the unsloth Qwen3-8B GGUF tree behind 4.68 GiB, the unsloth Qwen3-14B GGUF tree behind 8.38 GiB, the unsloth Devstral GGUF tree behind 13.35 GiB, and the unsloth Gemma 4 31B GGUF tree behind 17.07 GiB. Another quantiser’s Q4_K_M is a different file with a different byte size, so treat the mirror as part of the number.

Read the Devstral row before you buy: a 13.35 GiB file whose native context needs 20 GiB of cache on top. The weights fit 24 GB comfortably; the context does not.

Quantisation moves the left-hand term, not the right-hand one

Going from BF16 to Q4_K_M shrinks the file by roughly 3.3× for Qwen3-8B (15.26 GiB to 4.68 GiB). It does not touch the cache unless you also quantise the cache. With q8_0 packing — 32 elements in 34 bytes, 1.0625 bytes per element — the same 40,960-token context costs 2.99 GiB instead of 5.62, and the whole plan lands at 8.67 GiB including a 1 GiB allowance.

Ollama documents that this only works with Flash Attention enabled, and that the setting is global rather than per model (Ollama FAQ). A quantised cache type on a backend that cannot run Flash Attention is inert — the flag is accepted, the memory does not move. The CPU-only probe published with the budget article shows exactly that: the same slope with OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 until Flash Attention was turned on, then half.

Where the single-slope formula fails: Gemma 4 31B

Take the naive rule to Gemma 4 31B and you get 2 × 60 × 16 × 256 × 2 = 983,040 bytes per token, or 240 GiB at its 262,144-token maximum. That number is correct arithmetic and a wrong plan. The config declares a layer_types list in which only 10 of 60 layers are full attention, with global_head_dim 512 and 4 global KV heads; the other 50 slide over a 1,024-token window.

A sliding layer does not grow with context. It holds one window, ever. So the cost is a slope plus a fixed term:

  • 10 full layers: 2 × 10 × 4 × 512 × 2 = 81,920 bytes per token
  • 50 sliding layers: 2 × 50 × 16 × 256 × 2 × 1,024 = 800 MiB fixed, per slot
  • at 32,768 tokens: 2.50 GiB + 0.78 GiB = 3.28 GiB, not 30 GiB

This is the correction that matters most for 2026 models: if layer_types or sliding_window appears in a config, the per-token formula alone overestimates the cache by an order of magnitude, and a planner built on it will tell you a 24 GB card cannot run a 31B at 32k when the arithmetic says it can.

Largest context that fits, at a declared 1 GiB overhead

Computed with the same fixtures: file size plus f16 cache plus 1 GiB for compute buffers and CUDA context, capped at the model’s native context. If your runtime’s overhead is larger, subtract it and recompute — the planner does this for you.

Q4_K_M 8 GiB 12 GiB 16 GiB 24 GiB 48 GiB
Qwen3-8B 16,893 40,960 40,960 40,960 40,960
Qwen3-14B does not fit 17,170 40,960 40,960 40,960
Devstral-Small-2507 does not fit does not fit 10,813 63,242 131,072
Gemma 4 31B (hybrid) does not fit does not fit does not fit 67,485 262,144

Capped cells are written as the native context, not as the larger number the formula would allow. An 8 GiB card holds Qwen3-8B at 16,893 tokens and nothing else in this set; a 12 GB card holds it at the full 40,960 with about 0.7 GiB to spare, which is not a margin to plan a desktop session around once the display compositor takes its share.

Concurrency multiplies the cache, not the weights

Four parallel slots at 32,768 tokens on Qwen3-8B is 18 GiB of cache against 4.5 GiB for one slot — the weights are loaded once, the cache is allocated per slot. A server sized for one user’s long context is not sized for four users’ long contexts, and the difference is not in the file size anyone quotes.

The planner

plan.py reads a fixture of the four configs above and prints the breakdown, exiting non-zero on overflow so it can gate a launch script:

$ python3 plan.py --model qwen3-8b --quant Q4_K_M --context 40960 --vram 12
model    : qwen3-8b (Qwen/Qwen3-8B, native 40960 tokens, dense)
weights  : 4.68 GiB  (Q4_K_M GGUF file)
kv       : 5.62 GiB  (f16, 147,456 B/token x 40960)
overhead : 1.00 GiB  (declared allowance, not measured)
total    : 11.30 GiB
device   : 12.00 GiB  margin +0.70 GiB
verdict  : fits at the declared allowance

Full output of the two-slot run, unedited (the verdict line goes to stderr, so it prints before the buffered stdout when the terminal interleaves them):

$ python3 plan.py --model gemma-4-31b-it --quant Q4_K_M --context 32768 --parallel 2 --vram 24
model    : gemma-4-31b-it (google/gemma-4-31B-it, native 262144 tokens, hybrid)
weights  : 17.07 GiB  (Q4_K_M GGUF file)
kv       : 6.56 GiB  (f16, 81,920 B/token x 32768 + 0.78 GiB fixed window per slot, x2 slots)
overhead : 1.00 GiB  (declared allowance, not measured)
total    : 24.63 GiB
device   : 24.00 GiB  margin -0.63 GiB
verdict  : DOES NOT FIT - lower context, quantise the KV cache, or reduce parallel slots

Two slots on the hybrid model is the difference between fitting 24 GB and not: one slot totals 21.35 GiB, two slots 24.63 GiB.

Files, first-party and published with the article:

File What it is
plan.py The planner: weights + KV + declared overhead, hybrid-aware, non-zero exit on overflow
plan-fixtures.json The four configs and their published GGUF sizes, with the Qwen3-8B revision pinned
test_plan.py Six tests (14 assertions) pinning 147,456 B/token, 5.62 GiB at 40,960, the 4× slot multiplier and the hybrid fixed term

To add your own model, copy a config object into the fixtures file. The planner reads six fixture fields and nothing else; num_hidden_layers, num_key_value_heads, head_dim and gguf_gib drive the arithmetic, and the other two are for display:

  • num_hidden_layers, num_key_value_heads, head_dim — from the model’s config.json
  • max_position_embeddings — from config.json; printed in the header and used only to cap the “fits” search
  • gguf_gib — an object of {"Q4_K_M": 4.68, ...}, one entry per quant you intend to plan for, each value being the published file size in bytes divided by 1024³
  • repo — the model id, printed in the header; if you omit it the printer says repo not recorded instead of failing

hybrid is the only optional block, and it needs all five of full_layers, sliding_layers, window, global_head_dim, global_kv_heads. Add it only if the config carries layer_types or sliding_window: the mere presence of the key switches the model onto the hybrid branch, so a hybrid block invented for a dense model produces a wrong total rather than a denser one. revision is optional bookkeeping, never read by the arithmetic.

plan.py --list shows what loaded, and python3 plan.py --model <name> --quant <quant> --context <n> --vram <GiB> prints the breakdown and exits 1 when the total exceeds the card.

What this page does not establish

Every number above is arithmetic from published configs and file sizes, not an observed successful load: no GPU was available for this run. The formula itself was validated on a CPU-only host against a 0.5B model in the budget article — 11.98 KiB per token measured against 12.00 computed, and 6.37 against 6.38 for q8_0 with Flash Attention — which validates the arithmetic, not GPU behaviour, and not any large model.

Also out of scope: throughput, quality, tokens per second, vendor performance claims, whether a given runtime honours layer_types rather than allocating a uniform cache per layer, and vision projectors, which ship as separate mmproj files in the Gemma repositories and are not in any figure here.

Two gated repositories stayed gated: meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct reports gated: manual and both it and google/gemma-3-27b-it returned 401 for config.json from this host. Neither has a per-token figure here, and neither appears in any table above; the 70B is named only because it was the fifth repo the fixture plan asked for and could not be measured the same way.

If your runtime reports a served context shorter than the one you requested, that is a different failure from the one this page predicts — the truncation diagnosis and the overflow diagnosis cover it. Once the model fits, the payback model turns a throughput number into a purchase decision, and the model-list page is the place to choose between these four.

item.title: Your 18GB GGUF Is Not an 18GB Budget: Sizing KV Cache and Context for a Local Coding Model
item.description: A GGUF file is the weights, not the budget. Run the KV-cache formula before you download, with a measured 0.5B check against it on a 12 GB CPU host and the q8_0 setting that saves nothing without Flash Attention.
item.content:encoded:
You download a 4-bit quantised model, the file is roughly 18 GB, you have 24 GB of VRAM, and the arithmetic looks settled. Then the agent session gets long, the server either dies or quietly starts answering with a fraction of the context you asked for, and the model that “fit yesterday” no longer fits.

The missing term is the key/value cache. It is not in the GGUF file, it is not on the model card, and it is allocated by the runtime at load time from the context length you set — not from the number of tokens you happen to send. On the 12 GB CPU box used for the measurements below, the same 0.5B model occupied 417 MB of reported model memory at a 2,048-token context and 794 MB at 32,768, with an identical file on disk.

This article gives you one formula to run before downloading, one measured check of that formula that you can repeat, and one warning about a setting that looks like it halves memory and does not.

What the cache is, in one paragraph

Every transformer layer keeps, for every token in context, one key vector and one value vector per key/value head. The attention heads read them; they are not learned weights, they are state. The size is fixed by the model geometry and the cache element type:

bytes_per_token = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element

The 2 is key plus value. n_layers and n_kv_heads come from the model’s own config.json. head_dim is either an explicit field or hidden_size / num_attention_heads. bytes_per_element is 2 for f16 and about 1.0625 for q8_0, because q8_0 stores 32 values in 34 bytes — 8 bits each plus a scale.

Grouped-query attention is why this number is not as frightening as it looks. A model can have 64 attention heads and only 8 key/value heads; the cache scales with the second number. That is also why the per-token cost cannot be guessed from parameter count alone: two models of the same size can differ by 8x in cache cost depending on how aggressively they share KV heads.

Ollama’s own documentation fixes the default that catches people: “By default, Ollama uses a context window size of 4096 tokens”, overridable with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH or per request with num_ctx (Ollama FAQ). A coding agent session with file contents and tool output routinely exceeds that. Either the runtime truncates, or you raise the context and the cache grows with it.

Worked example one: the small model, measured

The tag used here is qwen2.5:0.5b at Q4_K_M. Its own config gives num_hidden_layers 24, num_key_value_heads 2, num_attention_heads 14 and hidden_size 896, so head_dim is 896 / 14 = 64 (Qwen2.5-0.5B config.json).

That yields 2 × 24 × 2 × 64 × 2 = 12,288 bytes per token, or 12.00 KiB. At a 32,768-token context the cache alone is 384 MiB — comparable to the model itself, on a model whose file is about 400 MB.

This is the shape of the problem in miniature: at a context the model advertises, the cache can be the same order of magnitude as the weights. Nobody notices on a 0.5B model because 384 MiB is noise. Scale the geometry up and the same term decides whether the card is big enough.

Worked example two: a 32B model, computed not measured

Take Qwen3-32B, whose config was fetched and read for this article: 64 layers, 64 attention heads, 8 key/value heads, head_dim 128, 40,960 maximum positions (Qwen3-32B config.json).

2 × 64 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 262,144 bytes per token = 256 KiB for f16. With q8_0 packing at 34 bytes per 32 elements the same geometry costs 136 KiB per token.

Context f16 cache q8_0 cache (with Flash Attention)
8,192 tokens 2 GiB 1.06 GiB
32,768 tokens 8 GiB 4.25 GiB
40,960 tokens 10 GiB 5.31 GiB

Every number in that table is computed from the config and the formula. None of it was measured on a 32B model — this host has no GPU and 12 GB of RAM. It is arithmetic you can redo in a spreadsheet in a minute, and that is the point: the term is predictable before you download anything.

Note what changed the number: not the parameter count, but 8 KV heads instead of 64, and a quantised cache. A dense 32B model without grouped-query attention would have cost eight times more per token and would not fit at that context on any consumer card.

The measured check on this machine

The probe starts a private Ollama server, forces one load per cell at a requested num_ctx, reads the runner’s VmRSS from /proc/<pid>/status, and confirms what the server actually honoured with ollama ps. Nothing else runs, so the only moving part is the cache allocation.

num_ctx KV type Flash Attention runner VmRSS ollama ps SIZE
2,048 f16 off 494,748 kB 417 MB
8,192 f16 off 567,752 kB 492 MB
32,768 f16 off 862,668 kB 794 MB
2,048 q8_0 off 494,220 kB 417 MB
8,192 q8_0 off 568,064 kB 492 MB
32,768 q8_0 off 862,896 kB 794 MB
8,192 q8_0 on 521,648 kB 442 MB
32,768 q8_0 on 678,308 kB 593 MB

The reported context matched the requested context in all eight rows, so no row is secretly a measurement of a different context.

From 2,048 to 32,768 tokens, f16 grew by 367,920 kB over 30,720 tokens: 11.98 KiB per token against 12.00 computed, an error of minus 0.20 percent. Subtracting the slope leaves a base of about 470 MB that barely moves across contexts (720 kB spread on eight rows), which is the Q4_K_M weights plus graph and allocator overhead. The slope is the portable part; the base is not.

The trap: a setting that looks like half the memory

OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 with default settings produced the same slope as f16: 12.00 KiB per token, 228 kB apart at 32,768 tokens, which is noise. The knob did nothing.

Ollama’s documentation says why, in the sentence most people skim: the K/V cache “can be quantized to significantly reduce memory usage when Flash Attention is enabled”. Re-running the same two cells with OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 halved the slope: 156,660 kB over 24,576 tokens is 6.37 KiB per token against 6.38 computed, and 0.532x the f16 slope. The saving is real — but only after the precondition is met.

Two practical consequences. First, verify a memory setting by its effect on resident memory, not by the name of the flag; a quantised cache type on a backend that cannot run Flash Attention is inert, and you will only find out when the box swaps. Second, compare slopes, not single readings: the base also moved with Flash Attention (567,752 kB to 521,648 kB at 8,192 tokens), so a one-point comparison would have been misleading in the opposite direction.

Turning it into a budget

The budget is three terms, and only one of them is on the download page:

resident ≈ weights (GGUF bytes) + KV cache at your context + runtime overhead

Work the numbers in the same unit before you buy anything. For a 32B-class model at a 32,768-token context, the cache term alone is 8 GiB at f16 or 4.25 GiB at q8_0 with Flash Attention. If your file is the 18 GB the title refers to — a figure this article takes from the reader’s rule of thumb and does not verify for any specific 31B release — then 18 + 8 + 2 GB of overhead is 28 GB, which does not fit a 24 GB card at full context. The same model with a quantised cache lands near 24 GB: still on the edge, and still not something to plan around without measuring your own box.

Three corrections that change the answer more often than a bigger GPU:

  • Parallel slots multiply the cache. OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL defaults to 1, and the docs state that required memory scales with it. A shared server sized for one user’s context is not sized for four.
  • The context default is 4,096, not the model’s maximum. A setup that “fit yesterday” may have fit because the runtime was quietly using a small context. Raising num_ctx to the model’s advertised maximum is where the memory goes.
  • Quantising the cache is not free of preconditions. It needs Flash Attention, which needs a backend and device that support it. Check the effect, not the flag.

When the total does not fit, the levers in order of cost are: lower the context to what the agent actually uses, quantise the cache if Flash Attention is available, reduce parallel slots, and only then move to a smaller model.

Doing it on your own machine in ten minutes

The probe is small enough to read before you run it. It starts its own server on a free loopback port so it does not disturb a running instance, samples the runner’s resident set after each load, records what ollama ps reports as the honoured context, and writes one CSV row per cell.

Files, all first-party and published with the article:

File What it is
kv_budget_probe.py The probe: context and cache-type matrix, RSS sampling, ollama ps cross-check
kv_budget_prompt.txt The fixed 30-token fixture with a head and a tail token, kept for replay and hashing; the probe sends a 1-token generation because the allocation happens at load
kv-budget-2026-11-01.csv The eight measured rows behind the table above
kv-budget-formula-check.md Measured slope against the config-derived slope, with the residual explained
method.md Server flags, sampling points, host, and what was deliberately not measured

Point it at a model that fits your box. Two cells are enough to get your own slope: the same cache type at two contexts, resident memory at each, difference divided by the context difference. If your slope is within a quarter of the formula, you can trust the arithmetic for the model you actually want; if it is not, the runtime is allocating something the formula does not describe and the formula’s answer for a bigger model is not safe to use.

What this does and does not establish

Measured, on one CPU-only host with one model tag: the cache is allocated at load from num_ctx, it grows linearly at the formula’s rate within 0.20 percent for f16 and 0.01 percent for q8_0 with Flash Attention, and the q8_0 setting is inert without Flash Attention.

Not measured, and not claimed: any throughput or tokens-per-second figure, any quality comparison, any GPU-backend behaviour, any multi-slot configuration, and any resident-memory number for a 32B or 27B model. The 32B figures are computed from its published config, and the 27B family is absent on purpose: the google/gemma-3-27b-it config returned HTTP 401 on both attempts, so its geometry is unverified here and no number for it appears in this article. One sample per cell was taken; repeat-run spread between identical configurations was 228 kB against a 368 MB slope, which is enough for a slope and not enough for sub-percent claims about the constant overhead.

The one-sentence version: the file you download is the smallest term in the budget, and the term that grows is the one nobody puts on the model card. Compute it before you download, then confirm it on your own machine with two loads.

If you have not chosen the model yet, the model-selection comparison and the coding-model shortlist are the better starting points; the inference-engineering guide explains PagedAttention and serving-side batching, which this article deliberately does not re-explain; and the 31B local setup guide covers the download half of the question.
